Override that dependency using `app.dependency_overrides`. This is the use case the docs describe: a provider might be charging you per request, and calling it might take some extra time than if you had a fixed mock user for tests.[1] In this case, you can override the dependency that calls that provider, and use a custom dependency that returns a mock user, only for your tests.[1]

**How it works:** your FastAPI application has an attribute `app.dependency_overrides`, it is a simple `dict`.[2] To override a dependency for testing, you put as a key the original dependency (a function), and as the value, your dependency override (another function).[2] And then FastAPI will call that override instead of the original dependency.[2] The original dependency won't run, nor any of the sub-dependencies it might have[1].

The example below is based on the docs, with the names changed to fit your case:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from .main import app, get_current_user

client = TestClient(app)


def override_get_current_user():
    return {"username": "testuser"}


app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user] = override_get_current_user
```

**Resetting:** you can reset your overrides (remove them) by setting `app.dependency_overrides` to be an empty `dict`[2]:

```python
app.dependency_overrides = {}
```

If you want to override a dependency only during some tests, you can set the override at the beginning of the test (inside the test function) and reset it at the end (at the end of the test function).[2]

The override works wherever the dependency is used. The original dependency could be used in a *path operation function*, a *path operation decorator* (when you don't use the return value), a `.include_router()` call, etc.[2]

More details: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/testing-dependencies/
